slides.title: Unit Outline
slides.body:
Unit Outline

Part 1: The neuromuscular junction
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue
Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: In this unit, we will begin by discussing the neuromuscular junction. Then, we will turn to the mechanisms underlying skeletal muscle fibre contraction and relaxation. Finally we will conclude with brief discussions of cardiac and smooth muscle, and how their function and regulation differ from that of skeletal muscle.

slides.title: Part 1: The neuromuscular junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The neuromuscular junction

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: We begin with Part 1: The neuromuscular junction.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Motor neuron stimulates muscle fibre at neuromuscular junction
changes the membrane potential (voltage)
triggers action potential which travels along sarcolemma

Muscle excitability. Adapted from: Ian Alexander, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The neuromuscular junction is the site where a motor neuron’s terminal meets a muscle fibre, and where that fibre first responds to that signaling. Every skeletal muscle fibre must be stimulated by a nerve ending at the neuromuscular junction so that a change in its membrane potential (also called voltage) occurs. This electrical change is necessary for subsequent contraction to occur.

Excitation signals from the neuron cause the generation an electrical current, called an action potential, in the sarcolemma (the plasma membrane) of the muscle fibre.

The action potential thus generated is linked to contraction, which is why the second requirement for skeletal muscular contraction is referred to as excitation-contraction coupling.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Resting membrane potential
all cells have membrane potentials (electric gradient across membrane)
at rest, inside is ~ -70 mV relative to outside

Resting Membrane Potential. From Unit 15.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: All living cells have membrane potentials, or electrical gradients across their membranes. The inside of the membrane is usually around -70 mV, relative to the outside. This is referred to as a cell’s resting membrane potential.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Currents
neurons and muscle fibres control membrane potential by regulating currents (flows of ions, and thus charge) across membrane, by opening and closing ion channels 
muscle fibres do so in response to neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh) from motor neurons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Ligand-Gated Channels. From Unit 15.
slides.notes: Neurons and muscle cells can use their membrane potentials to generate electrical signals. They do this by controlling the movement of charged ions across their membranes to create electrical currents. This is achieved by opening and closing specialized proteins in the membrane called ion channels. Muscle fibres do so in response to the neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh) from motor neurons.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Action potentials
occur in neurons and muscle fibres
special type of electrical signal that can travel along a cell membrane as a wave of depolarization
allows a signal to be transmitted quickly and faithfully over long distances

Action potential propogation. Credit: Laurentaylorj, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Both neurons and skeletal muscle cells are electrically excitable, meaning that they are able to generate action potentials. An action potential is a special type of electrical signal that can travel along a cell membrane as a wave of depolarization (the inside of the membrane becomes less negative, and at times even positive relative to the outside). This allows a signal to be transmitted quickly and faithfully over long distances.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Excitation-contraction coupling 
for a skeletal muscle fibre to contract…          
…its membrane must first be “excited” to fire an action potential
coupling of action potential and contraction is via release of Ca2+ from sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)
the calcium ions interact with components of the sarcomeres, initiating muscle contraction

Excitation-contraction coupling

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Excitation-contraction coupling 

Although the term excitation-contraction coupling confuses some, it comes down to this: for a skeletal muscle fibre to contract, its membrane must first be “excited”—in other words, it must be stimulated to fire an action potential.

The muscle fibre’s action potential, which sweeps along the sarcolemma as a wave, is “coupled” to the actual contraction through the release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of the fibre.

The calcium then interacts with components of the myofibril’s sarcomeres, initiating muscle contraction.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Presynaptic side:
neuronal action potential reaches each neuromuscular junction (synapse / synaptic cleft)
local membrane potential depolarized, opening Ca2+ channels
Ca2+ influx triggers vesicles to fuse with membrane, releasing ACh

Motor End-Plate and Innervation.

Calcium-triggered Neurotransmitter Release. Adapted from figure in Unit 15.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Let’s look at this in more detail…

Calcium ions are actually also involved on the presynaptic side, within the motor neuron. Signaling begins when a neuronal action potential travels along the axon of a motor neuron, and then along the individual branches of the axon, terminating at individual neuromuscular junctions. Depolarization of the membrane potential causes calcium channels in the membrane of the neuron to open, allowing calcium ions to diffuse into the neuron’s cytosol. This influx of calcium causes vesicles in the neuron to fuse with its plasma membrane, releasing their contents – the neurotransmitter acetylcholine – into the space between the neuron and the muscle fibre, called the synaptic cleft.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Postsynaptic side:
ACh binds to cholinergic receptors of motor end-plate (postsynaptic membrane of skeletal muscle)
opens ligand-gated ion channel within receptor
Na+ cations enter, depolarizing sarcolemma

Motor End-Plate and Innervation. At the neuromuscular junction, the axon terminal releases acetylcholine. The motor end-plate is the location of the acetylcholine-receptors in the muscle fibre sarcolemma. When acetylcholine molecules are released, they diffuse across a minute space called the synaptic cleft and bind to the receptors.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Thus, the associated axon terminal at each neuromuscular junction releases acetylcholine. The acetylcholine molecules diffuse across the minute space of the synaptic cleft and bind to cholinergic receptors (the name for acetylcholine receptors) located within the motor end-plate of the sarcolemma on the other side of the synapse. Once acetylcholine binds, a channel in the acetylcholine receptor (called a ligand-gated ion channel because binding of a ligand to the receptor triggers it) opens and positively charged sodium ions can pass through into the muscle fibre, causing it to depolarize.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Postsynaptic side, continued:
depolarization of sarcolemma opens voltage-gated sodium channels
action potential spreads from motor end plate, along sarcolemma
after depolarization, membrane repolarized (again hyperpolarized)
ACh in synaptic cleft degraded by the enzyme acetylcholinesterase (AChE), turning off receptor to avoid overexcitation and contraction
to extend a muscle contraction, more acetylcholine must be released by the motor neuron

Excitation-contraction coupling

Action potential propogation. Adapted from: Laurentaylorj, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Acetylcholinesterase degrades acetylcholine. Adapted from: Sbolmer, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As the membrane depolarizes, another set of ion channels called voltage-gated sodium channels are triggered to open. Sodium ions enter the muscle fibre along further and further stretches of sarcolemma as the action potential rapidly spreads (or “fires”) along the entire membrane.

Immediately following depolarization of a segment of membrane, that segment repolarizes (again becomes hyperpolarized, re-establishing the negative membrane potential). 

Meanwhile, the acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft is degraded by the enzyme acetylcholinesterase so that the acetylcholine can no longer bind to an acetylcholine receptor, thereby avoiding unwanted extended muscle excitation and contraction. To extend a muscle contraction, more acetylcholine must be released by the motor neuron.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Postsynaptic side, continued:
to reach SR, action potential travels down invaginations called transverse tubules (T-tubules)
a T-tubule plus SR membranes on either side of it is called triad
triads surround myofibrils, which contain actin and myosin
action potentials open up voltage-gated channels that connect sarcolemma of t-tubule to sarcoplasmic reticulum

Excitation-contraction coupling

The T-tubule. Narrow T-tubules permit the conduction of electrical impulses. The SR functions to regulate intracellular levels of calcium. Two terminal cisternae (where enlarged SR connects to the T-tubule) and one T-tubule comprise a triad—a “threesome” of membranes, with those of SR on two sides and the T-tubule sandwiched between them.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Propagation of an action potential along the sarcolemma is still part of the excitation portion of excitation-contraction coupling; it is this excitation that triggers the release of calcium ions from storage in the skeletal muscle cell’s sarcoplasmic reticulum. For the action potential to reach the membrane of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, there are periodic invaginations that run deep within the sarcolemma, called transverse tubules (or T-tubules). 

A T-tubule along with sarcoplasmic reticulum membranes on either side of it is referred to as a triad. Triads surround and enclose the cylindrical structure known as a myofibril, which contains actin and myosin.

slides.title: Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction
slides.body:
Part 1: The Neuromuscular Junction

Postsynaptic side, continued:
action potential within t-tubule causes opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in SR membrane
Ca2+ diffuses out of SR, into sarcoplasm, initiating contraction

_  _  _  _  _  _  _  _  _  _

+ + + +

+ + + +

Contraction of a Muscle Fibre. A cross-bridge forms between actin and the myosin heads triggering contraction. As long as Ca2+ ions remain in the sarcoplasm to bind to troponin, and as long as ATP is available, the muscle fibre will continue to shorten.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: T-tubules thus carry the action potential into the interior of the cell. The action potential triggers the opening of calcium channels coupled to voltage-sensitive proteins. These are located in the membrane of an adjacent sarcoplasmic reticulum. Opening these channels causes calcium ions to diffuse out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum and into the sarcoplasm. It is the arrival of calcium in the sarcoplasm that initiates contraction of the muscle fibre by contraction of its contractile units, the sarcomeres.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: We now turn to Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Contraction:
Tropomyosin – long molecule, blocks myosin-binding sites on actin
Troponin – has binding site for Ca2+, keeps tropomyosin in place in absence of Ca2+
when Ca2+ binds troponin, troponin changes conformation & loses hold on tropomyosin, exposing myosin-binding sites on actin
myosin heads bind the actin, forming cross-bridges, pulling actin toward centre of each sarcomere, contracting muscle
ATP hydrolysis powers cross-bridge cycling and sarcomere contraction

Contraction of a Muscle Fibre. A cross-bridge forms between actin and the myosin heads triggering contraction. As long as Ca2+ ions remain in the sarcoplasm to bind to troponin, and as long as ATP is available, the muscle fibre will continue to shorten.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As mentioned in the previous section, it is the calcium ions that initiate contraction. Let’s look at the mechanisms in the sarcomeres of the myofibrils in more detail.

Troponin and tropomyosin are the two major proteins that regulate skeletal muscle contraction. Tropomyosin is a long, rod-like molecule which shields (or blocks) the myosin-binding sites on actin. Troponin, which has a binding site for calcium, is a globular protein whose role is to keep the longer, tropomyosin in its place.

Upon binding of calcium to troponin, troponin changes its conformation (its overall three-dimensional shape) and loses its hold on tropomyosin, thereby exposing the myosin-binding sites on actin. This allows myosin heads to bind the actin, forming cross-bridges.

ATP is then hydrolyzed to power cross-bridge cycling and the pulling of actin strands inward by myosin.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Sliding filament model:
image of sarcomere shortening
note myosin heads forming cross-bridges
actin attached to Z-disc/line
myosin attached to M-line
myosin pulls actin toward centre of sarcomere
sarcomeres, arranged in series, cause muscle to shorten (contract)
Note: each myosin head can only pull a very short distance before reaching its limit
must be “re-cocked” to pull again, requiring ATP

Types of muscle. Adapted from: www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Here is an image of sarcomere shortening. Note the cross-bridge formation in the lower panel, where myosin heads serve to connect the myosin with the actin. Actin filaments, anchored at their ends by the Z-discs, do not extend completely into the central region, which only contains myosin filaments, themselves anchored at a spot called the M-line. 

Once cross-bridges are formed, and assuming ATP is present to power the mechanical motion, myosin pulls the actin toward the centre of the sarcomere. This process is known as the sliding filament model of muscle contraction.

Since the sarcomeres are lined up in series, and each myofibril shortens within an excited muscle fibre, the result is that the entire muscle will shorten.

Each myosin head can only pull a very short distance before it has reached its limit and must be “re-cocked” before it can pull again, a step that requires ATP.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

ATP and muscle contraction 
cross-bridge cycle – myosin heads must pull actin, detach, re-cock, attach to new sites, pull, detach, re-cock, etc. – requires ATP
ATP hydrolysis cocks (changes angle of) the myosin head so that it can bind to the actin binding site
ADP and Pi are released as the myosin head moves toward the M-line, pulling the actin with it = power stroke
new ATP binding needed to detach myosin heads from actin
rigor mortis occurs after death, in absence of ATP

Skeletal Muscle Contraction. (a) The active site on actin is exposed as calcium binds to troponin. (b) The myosin head is attracted to actin, and myosin binds actin at its actin-binding site, forming the cross-bridge. (c) During the power stroke, the phosphate generated in the previous contraction cycle is released. This results in the myosin head pivoting toward the center of the sarcomere, after which the attached ADP is released. (d) A new molecule of ATP attaches to the myosin head, causing the cross-bridge to detach. (e) The myosin head hydrolyzes ATP to ADP and phosphate, which returns the myosin to the cocked position.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Thus, for thin filaments to continue to slide past thick filaments during muscle contraction, myosin heads must pull the actin at the binding sites, detach, re-cock, attach to more binding sites, pull, detach, re-cock, etc. This repeated movement is known as the cross-bridge cycle.

Each cross-bridge cycle requires energy, which is provided by ATP. ATP hydrolysis changes the shape of the myosin head so that it can bind to the actin binding site.

Cross-bridge formation occurs when the myosin head attaches to the actin while adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and inorganic phosphate (Pi) are still bound to it. Both are released as the myosin head moves toward the M-line, pulling the actin along with it. This movement is called the power stroke. 

ATP binding (not hydrolysis, but just its binding as a ligand) causes the myosin head to detach from the actin. In the absence of ATP, the myosin head will not detach from actin, causing a locking up of the muscle at its current length. This occurs after death, in the condition known as rigor mortis.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Relaxation:
motor neuron release of ACh stops (and AChE degrades existing ACh)
ligand-gated sodium channels on the motor end-plate close
action potentials down t-tubules cease
Ca2+ channels in SR close
Ca2+ pumped back into SR (uses ATP)
tropomyosin reshields binding sites on the actin 
after ATP causes myosin to let go of actin
elastic fibres return muscle to its resting length
running out of ATP also stops contraction (fatigue)

Relaxation of a Muscle Fibre. Calcium ions are pumped back into the SR, which causes the tropomyosin to reshield the binding sites on the actin strands. A muscle may also stop contracting when it runs out of ATP and becomes fatigued.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Muscle contraction usually stops when signaling from the motor neuron ends. Recall that acetylcholinesterase degrades acetylcholine within the synapse. This causes the closure of ligand-gated sodium channels on the motor end-plate. This causes a cessation of action potentials traveling along the sarcolemma and T-tubules, and the repolarization of those membranes closes the voltage-gated calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium ions are then pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which causes the tropomyosin to reshield (or re-cover) the binding sites on the actin strands. This causes myosin to let go of the actin, and the elastic fibres of the muscle return it to its resting length.

This pumping of calcium, against its concentration gradient, back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum is a process that requires ATP hydrolysis. 

Note that a muscle also can stop contracting if it runs out of ATP and becomes fatigued.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Sources of ATP
ATP stores in muscle are low, only enough to power contraction for a few seconds
must be regenerated quickly 
3 mechanisms for ATP regeneration:
creatine phosphate metabolism
glycolysis and lactic acid fermentation (anaerobic)
cellular respiration (aerobic)

ATP molecules store energy from metabolism of food molecules, and transfer that energy to other bodily processes when ATP is split to ADP and a phosphate group. Credit: Lisawerner9, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Sources of ATP

Muscle contraction does not occur without sufficient amounts of ATP. The amount of ATP stored in muscle is very low, only sufficient to power a few seconds worth of contractions. Therefore, as it is broken down, ATP must be regenerated and replaced quickly to allow for sustained contraction: ATP can be regenerated through three mechanisms: creatine phosphate metabolism, an anaerobic pathway (involving glycolysis and lactic acid formation) and aerobic cellular respiration.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Creatine phosphate
when at rest, excess ATP is used to form creatine phosphate
ATP broken down to ADP + Pi
Pi added to creatine
creatine phosphate can later be hydrolyzed, regenerating ATP from ADP
reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme creatine kinase
provides a few extra seconds of energy for muscle contraction

Muscle Metabolism. (a) Some ATP is stored in a resting muscle. As contraction starts, it is used up in seconds. More ATP is generated from creatine phosphate for about 15 seconds..

Creatine supplements. Adapted from: Ganesh Mohan T, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Creatine phosphate is a molecule that can store energy in its phosphate bonds. In a resting muscle, excess ATP transfers its energy to creatine, creating creatine phosphate and ADP. The creatine phosphate acts as an energy reserve that can be used to quickly create more ATP. When the muscle starts to contract and needs energy, creatine phosphate transfers its phosphate back to ADP to reform ATP and creatine. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme creatine kinase and occurs very quickly; thus, creatine phosphate-derived ATP powers about 15 seconds of muscle contraction after the initial ATP is used up. However, another energy source has to be used to continue muscle contraction beyond that point… this additional source of ATP will be glycolysis, as described on the next slide.

First, however, I often get asked about creating supplements for building muscle, and thus wanted to briefly touch on this topic. Studies of this practice indicate that the additional creatine may provide an extra second or two of ATP during intense exercise. Whether this provides meaningful benefits is debatable.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

The Anaerobic Pathway
glycolysis is an anaerobic (non-oxygen-dependent) process that breaks down glucose (sugar) to produce ATP
later ATP source than creatine phosphate
uses glucose (free or hydrolyzed from glycogen)
1 glucose broken to 2 pyruvic acids, and produces 2 ATP
pyruvic acid can be used in aerobic respiration (when oxygen is available) or converted to lactic acid (when oxygen levels are low)
lactic acid fermentation – conversion to lactic acid allows for recycling of the coenzyme NAD+ from NADH – needed for glycolysis to continue
anaerobic pathway generates ATP for ~1 min - used for intense bursts of energy

Muscle Metabolism. (b) Each glucose molecule produces two ATP and two molecules of pyruvic acid, which can be used in aerobic respiration or converted to lactic acid. If oxygen is not available, pyruvic acid is converted to lactic acid, which may contribute to muscle fatigue. This occurs during strenuous exercise when high amounts of energy are needed but oxygen cannot be sufficiently delivered to muscle.

Lactic acid fermentation. Adapted from: Lisawerner9, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The Anaerobic Pathway

As the ATP produced by creatine phosphate is depleted, muscles turn to glycolysis as an ATP source. Glycolysis is an anaerobic (meaning non-oxygen-dependent) process that breaks down glucose to produce ATP. The sugar used in glycolysis can be provided by blood glucose or by metabolizing glycogen that is stored in the muscle. The breakdown of one glucose molecule produces two ATP and two molecules of pyruvic acid, which can be used either in aerobic respiration if sufficient oxygen is available, or when oxygen levels are low, converted to lactic acid. 

This conversion to lactic acid is called lactic acid fermentation, and it is important under low oxygen conditions, as it allows the recycling of the coenzyme NAD+ from NADH. NAD+ is needed for glycolysis to continue. This conversion occurs during strenuous exercise when high amounts of energy are needed but oxygen cannot be sufficiently delivered to muscle. Glycolysis itself cannot be sustained for very long (approximately one minute of muscle activity), but it is useful in facilitating short bursts of high-intensity output.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Aerobic cellular respiration
glucose OR other nutrients (incl. pyruvic acid)
takes place in mitochondria 
requires O2
some stored locally bound to myoglobin
remaining comes via blood
oxidative muscles are thin, so that O2 can diffuse in; also possess much vascularization and many mitochondria
produces CO2, H20, and many ATP (~32-34 vs. only 2 from glycolysis)

Muscle Metabolism. (c) Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen (O2) to produce carbon dioxide, water, and ATP. Approximately 95 percent of the ATP required for resting or moderately active muscles is provided by aerobic respiration, which takes place in mitochondria.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Aerobic cellular respiration

Aerobic cellular respiration is the breakdown of glucose or other nutrients in the presence of oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water, and ATP. Approximately 95% of the ATP required for resting or moderately active muscles is provided by aerobic respiration, which takes place in mitochondria. The inputs for aerobic respiration include glucose circulating in the bloodstream, pyruvic acid, and fatty acids. Aerobic respiration is much more efficient than anaerobic glycolysis, producing approximately 32 to 34 ATPs per molecule of glucose versus two from glycolysis. However, aerobic respiration cannot be sustained without a steady supply of oxygen to the skeletal muscle. 

To help with the oxygen supply, muscles store a small amount of excess oxygen bound to a protein called myoglobin, allowing for more efficient muscle contractions and less fatigue. Because the remaining oxygen needs to diffuse into the muscle from the bloodstream, muscles that rely on aerobic cellular respiration (that is, oxidative muscles), cannot be too large, or the distance for diffusion would be too far. Furthermore, such muscles have high blood vascularization, and possess many mitochondria.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Skeletal muscle types:
slow oxidative (SO) fibres
contract slowly (“slow twitch”) due to slow ATPase
use aerobic respiration
fast oxidative (FO) fibres (a.k.a., fast oxidative glycolytic)
contract quickly (“fast twitch”) due to fast ATPase
primarily use aerobic respiration
may switch to anaerobic respiration so can fatigue more quickly than SO fibres
fast glycolytic (FG) fibres
contract quickly (“fast twitch”) due to fast ATPase
primarily use anaerobic glycolysis
most skeletal muscles contain all three types, although in varying proportions
different types of exercise can shift their proportions

Gaining FO muscle running marathons. Credit: Petar Milošević, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Gaining FG muscle. Arnold Schwarzenegger in body builder days. Credit: Madison Square Garden Center, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Two criteria to consider when classifying the types of muscle fibres are how fast some fibres contract relative to others, and how they produce ATP. The speed of contraction is dependent on how quickly myosin’s ATPase hydrolyzes ATP to produce cross-bridge cycling. Fast fibres hydrolyze ATP approximately twice as quickly as slow fibres, resulting in “fast-twitch” muscles with much quicker cross-bridge cycling than “slow twitch” fibres. The primary metabolic pathway used by a muscle fibre determines whether the fibre is classified as oxidative or glycolytic. If a fibre primarily produces ATP through aerobic pathways it is oxidative, and produces ATP for a long time. Glycolytic fibres primarily create ATP through anaerobic glycolysis, and thus fatigue quickly, though they tend to be larger and stronger than oxidative fibres. 

Using these criteria, there are three main classifications of skeletal muscle fibres. Slow oxidative fibres contract relatively slowly and use aerobic respiration to produce ATP. Fast oxidative fibres have fast contractions and primarily use aerobic respiration, but they may switch to anaerobic respiration, and so they tend to fatigue more quickly than do slow oxidative fibres. Lastly, fast glycolytic fibres have fast contractions and primarily use anaerobic glycolysis. The fast glycolytic fibres are stronger but fatigue more quickly than the others. 

Most skeletal muscles contain all three types, although in varying proportions. Different types of exercise can shift their proportions.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Motor units
small motor units
motor neuron connects to only a few muscle fibres
weak but precise movement
e.g., eye muscles, fingers
large motor unit
motor neuron connects to many muscle fibres
strong but “gross” movement
e.g., limbs, back
can recruit few or many of these motor units

Motor unit recruitment. Credit: Daniel Walsh and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As you have learned, every skeletal muscle fibre must be innervated by the axon terminal of a motor neuron in order to contract. Each muscle fibre is innervated by only one motor neuron. The actual group of muscle fibres, within a given muscle, that are innervated by a single motor neuron is called a motor unit. The size of a motor unit is variable depending on the nature of the muscle.

A small motor unit is an arrangement where a single motor neuron recruits a small number of muscle fibres in a muscle. Small motor units permit very fine motor control of the muscle. The best examples in humans are the small motor units of the extraocular eye muscles that move the eyeballs. There are thousands of muscle fibres in each muscle, but every six or so fibres are supplied by a single motor neuron, as the axons branch to form synaptic connections at their individual neuromuscular junctions. This allows for exquisite control of eye movements so that both eyes can quickly focus on the same object. Small motor units are also involved in the many fine movements of the fingers and thumb of the hand for grasping, texting, etc.

A large motor unit is an arrangement where a single motor neuron supplies a large number of muscle fibres in a muscle. Large motor units are concerned with simple, or “gross,” movements, such as powerfully extending the knee joint. The best examples are the large motor units of the thigh muscles or back muscles, where a single motor neuron will supply thousands of muscle fibres in a muscle, as its axon splits into thousands of branches.

To regulate the strength of contraction, you can recruit only a few, or many of these motor units within a given muscle. In the diagram here, a weak contraction would involve activation of solely motor neuron 1. A medium strength contraction would be triggered by activating motor neurons 1 and 2. And a strong muscle contraction would involve the activation of motor neurons 1, 2, and 3.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Motor units
small motor units
smaller, lower-threshold motor neurons that are more excitable (fire first)
connected to smaller muscle fibres
larger motor units
neurons have higher action potential thresholds (need more stimulation from brain centres)
connected to larger muscle fibres

Motor unit recruitment. Credit: Daniel Walsh and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Typically, the small motor units in the muscle will have smaller, lower-threshold motor neurons that are more excitable, firing first to their skeletal muscle fibres, which also tend to be the smallest. Activation of these smaller motor units, results in a relatively small degree of contractile strength (a.k.a., tension) generated in the muscle. 

As more strength is needed, larger motor units, with bigger, higher-threshold motor neurons are enlisted to activate larger muscle fibres. This increasing activation of motor units produces an increase in muscle contraction known as recruitment. As more motor units are recruited, the muscle contraction grows progressively stronger. In some muscles, the largest motor units may generate a contractile force of 50 times more than the smallest motor units in the muscle. This allows a feather to be picked up using the biceps brachii arm muscle with minimal force, and a heavy weight to be lifted by the same muscle by recruiting the largest motor units.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Muscle tension – force generated by muscle
isotonic contractions – load is moved as the length of the muscle shortens
concentric contraction – muscle shortens to move a load
e.g., curling weight upward
eccentric contraction – muscle tension diminishes and the muscle lengthens 
e.g., lowering weight in controlled manner
isometric contraction – muscle produces tension without changing the angle of a skeletal joint
e.g., pushing against side of a building

Types of Muscle Contractions. During isotonic contractions, muscle length changes to move a load. During isometric contractions, muscle length does not change because the load exceeds the tension the muscle can generate.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
To move a load, the sarcomeres in the muscle fibres of the skeletal muscle must shorten. The force generated by the contraction of the muscle (or shortening of the sarcomeres) is called muscle tension. However, muscle tension also is generated when the muscle is contracting against a load that does not move, resulting in two main types of skeletal muscle contractions: isotonic contractions and isometric contractions.

In isotonic contractions, where the tension in the muscle stays constant, a load is moved as the length of the muscle changes. There are two types of isotonic contractions: concentric and eccentric. A concentric contraction involves the muscle shortening to move a load. An example of this is the biceps brachii muscle contracting when a hand weight is brought upward with increasing muscle tension. As the biceps brachii contract, the angle of the elbow joint decreases as the forearm is brought toward the body. An eccentric contraction occurs as the muscle tension diminishes and the muscle lengthens. In this case, the hand weight is lowered in a slow and controlled manner as the amount of cross-bridges being activated by nervous system stimulation decreases. In this case, as tension is released from the biceps brachii, the angle of the elbow joint increases. 

An isometric contraction occurs as the muscle produces tension without changing the angle of a skeletal joint. Isometric contractions involve sarcomere shortening and increasing muscle tension, but do not move a load, as the force produced cannot overcome the resistance provided by the load. For example, if one attempts to lift a hand weight that is too heavy, there will be sarcomere activation and shortening to a point, and ever-increasing muscle tension, but no change in the angle of the elbow joint. In everyday living, isometric contractions are active in maintaining posture and maintaining bone and joint stability. However, holding your head in an upright position occurs not because the muscles cannot move the head, but because the goal is to remain stationary and not produce movement. 

Most actions of the body are the result of a combination of isotonic and isometric contractions working together to produce a wide range of outcomes.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Length-tension range of a sarcomere
cross-bridges form where thin and thick filaments overlap
maximal tension produced at 80-120% resting length
@ >120%, less overlap of actin and myosin, so force decreases
@ <80%, actins overlap so do not contact as many myosin heads, force decreases; eventually no more movement possible

The Ideal Length of a Sarcomere. Sarcomeres produce maximal tension when thick and thin filaments overlap between about 80 percent to 120 percent.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Length-Tension Range of a Sarcomere

When a skeletal muscle fiber contracts, myosin heads attach to actin to form cross-bridges followed by the thin filaments sliding over the thick filaments as the heads pull the actin, and this results in sarcomere shortening, creating the tension of the muscle contraction. The cross-bridges can only form where thin and thick filaments already overlap, so that the length of the sarcomere has a direct influence on the force generated when the sarcomere shortens. This is called the length-tension relationship.

The ideal length of a sarcomere to produce maximal tension occurs at 80 percent to 120 percent of its resting length. This length maximizes the overlap of actin-binding sites and myosin heads. If a sarcomere is stretched beyond this ideal length (past 120 percent), thick and thin filaments do not overlap sufficiently, which results in less tension produced. If a sarcomere is shortened beyond 80 percent, the zone of overlap is reduced with the thin filaments jutting beyond the last of the myosin heads. Eventually, there is nowhere else for the thin filaments to go and the amount of tension is diminished.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Frequency of motor neuron stimulation
single action potential of motor neuron = single contraction of muscle fibers of motor unit, a twitch
a single twitch is very short in duration
does not accomplish significant muscle movement
more like a muscle shiver

A Myogram of a Muscle Twitch. A single muscle twitch has a latent period, a contraction phase when tension increases, and a relaxation phase when tension decreases. During the latent period, the action potential is being propagated along the sarcolemma. During the contraction phase, Ca++ ions in the sarcoplasm bind to troponin, tropomyosin moves from actin-binding sites, cross-bridges between actin and myosin form, and sarcomeres shorten. During the relaxation phase, tension decreases as Ca++ ions are pumped out of the sarcoplasm and cross-bridge cycling stops.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Frequency of Motor Neuron Stimulation

A single action potential from a motor neuron will produce a single contraction in the muscle fibers of its motor unit. This isolated contraction is called a twitch. 

Although a person can experience a muscle “twitch,” a single twitch does not produce any significant muscle activity in a living body. It is more like a shiver when you are cold.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Summation and tetanus
series of action potentials to the muscle fibers is necessary to produce a muscle contraction that can produce work
wave summation – if fibers are stimulated while previous twitch is still occurring, the second twitch will be stronger
second stimulus triggers release of more Ca2+, which activates more sarcomeres
tetanus – high frequency of motor neuron signaling, relaxation phase disappears completely

Wave Summation and Tetanus. (a) The excitation-contraction coupling effects of successive motor neuron signaling is added together which is referred to as wave summation. The bottom of each wave, the end of the relaxation phase, represents the point of stimulus. (b) When the stimulus frequency is so high that the relaxation phase disappears completely, the contractions become continuous; this is called tetanus.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A series of action potentials to the muscle fibers is necessary to produce a muscle contraction that can produce work. 

The rate at which a motor neuron fires action potentials affects the tension produced in the skeletal muscle. If the fibers are stimulated while a previous twitch is still occurring, the second twitch will be stronger. This response is called wave summation, because the excitation-contraction coupling effects of successive motor neuron signaling are summed, or added together. At the molecular level, summation occurs because the second stimulus triggers the release of more calcium ions, which become available to activate additional sarcomeres while the muscle is still contracting from the first stimulus. Summation results in greater contraction of the motor unit.

If the frequency of motor neuron signaling increases so high that the relaxation phase disappears completely, contractions become continuous in a process called tetanus.

slides.title: Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation
slides.body:
Part 2: Skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation

Muscle tone
continuous partial contraction of a muscle at rest
causes the muscle to resist passive stretch
allows muscles to continually stabilize joints and maintain posture
Muscle size
although muscle cells can change in size, new cells are not formed when muscles grow
hypertrophy – structural proteins added, muscle fibres increase in diameter
atrophy – structural proteins lost, muscle mass decreases 
sarcopenia – muscle atrophy with age
fibres replaced with connective & adipose tissue
can be delayed to some extent by exercise

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Atrophy. Muscle mass is reduced as muscles atrophy with disuse.
slides.notes:
Muscle tone

Skeletal muscles are rarely completely relaxed, or flaccid. Even if a muscle is not producing movement, it is contracted a small amount to maintain a muscle tone. The tension produced by muscle tone allows muscles to continually stabilize joints and maintain posture.

Muscle Atrophy

Physical training alters the appearance of skeletal muscles and can produce changes in muscle performance. Conversely, a lack of use can result in decreased performance and muscle appearance. Although muscle cells can change in size, new cells are not formed when muscles grow. Instead, structural proteins are added to a muscle fibre in a process called hypertrophy, so cell diameter increases. The reverse, when structural proteins are lost and muscle mass decreases, is called atrophy.

Muscle atrophy with age, referred to as sarcopenia, is irreversible. This is a primary reason why even highly trained athletes succumb to declining performance with age. This decline is noticeable in athletes whose sports require strength and powerful movements, such as sprinting, whereas the effects of age are less noticeable in endurance athletes such as marathon runners or long-distance cyclists. As muscles age, muscle fibres die, and they are replaced by connective tissue and adipose tissue. Because those tissues cannot contract and generate force as muscle can, muscles lose the ability to produce powerful contractions. The decline in muscle mass causes a loss of strength, including the strength required for posture and mobility. Sarcopenia can be delayed to some extent by exercise, as training adds structural proteins and causes cellular changes that can offset the effects of atrophy. Increased exercise can produce greater numbers of cellular mitochondria, increase capillary density, and increase the mass and strength of connective tissue.

slides.title: Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: We now move on to Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue.

slides.title: Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue

Cardiac myocyte histology:
striated
organized into sarcomeres
shorter than skeletal muscle
uninucleate
possess many mitochondria and myoglobin (ATP produced primarily by aerobic metabolism)
extensively branched; connected by intercalated discs – allows for synchronized contraction of atria and then ventricles

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Cardiac muscle tissue employs highly coordinated contractions to pump blood into the vessels of the circulatory system. Recall that similar to skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle is striated and organized into sarcomeres, possessing the same banding organization as skeletal muscle. However, cardiac muscle fibres are shorter than skeletal muscle fibres because they do not develop from developmental fusion of myoblasts. They thus usually contain only one nucleus. 

What we have not yet covered is that cardiac muscle fibres, similarly to skeletal muscle fibres, also possess many mitochondria and many myoglobin molecules, as ATP is produced primarily through aerobic metabolism. Cardiac muscle fibre cells are also extensively branched and are connected to one another by intercalated discs. An intercalated disc allows the cardiac muscle cells to contract in a synchronized pattern so that the heart can work as a pump.

slides.title: Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue

Gap Junctions and Desmosomes
intercalated discs are part of sarcolemma
contain gap junctions and desmosomes
gap junctions – forms channels between adjacent cardiac muscle fibres, allows depolarizing current to flow between cells (electric coupling)
creates functional unit of contraction called a syncytium
desmosome – cell structure that anchors ends of cardiac muscle fibres together, so cells do not pull apart during contraction

Cardiac Muscle. Intercalated discs are part of the cardiac muscle sarcolemma and they contain gap junctions and desmosomes.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Intercalated discs are part of the sarcolemma and contain two structures important in cardiac muscle contraction: gap junctions and desmosomes. A gap junction forms channels between adjacent cardiac muscle fibres that allow the depolarizing current produced by cations to flow from one cardiac muscle cell to the next. This joining is called electric coupling (as opposed to excitation-contraction coupling), and in cardiac muscle it allows the quick transmission of action potentials and the coordinated contraction of the entire heart.  This network of electrically connected cardiac muscle cells creates a functional unit of contraction called a syncytium. 

The remainder of the intercalated disc is composed of desmosomes. A desmosome is a cell structure that anchors the ends of cardiac muscle fibres together so the cells do not pull apart during the stress of individual fibres contracting.

slides.title: Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue

Electrical coupling
contractions of the heart (heartbeats) are controlled by specialized cardiac muscle cells called pacemaker cells
respond to signals from hormones and the autonomic nervous system to increase or decrease heart rate via frequency of action potentials
this then also affects blood pressure
The functional syncytium (wave of contraction)
pacemaker exhibit autorhythmicity (cells are self-excitable – depolarize to threshold, then fire APs)
depolarization travels to adjacent cells via gap junctions, causing contractions at rate of APs
one (prolonged) AP = 1 heart beat
no tetanus, as holding contraction of cardiac myocytes would be dangerous

Electrical signaling through heart. Credit: JHeuser assumed (based on copyright claims)., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Electrical Coupling

Contractions of the heart (heartbeats) are controlled by specialized cardiac muscle cells called pacemaker cells that directly control heart rate. These pacemaker cells respond to signals from the autonomic nervous system to increase or decrease heart rate. The pacemaker cells can also respond to various hormones with the effect of modulating heart rate and thus also controlling blood pressure.

The Functional Syncytium

The functional syncytium (the wave of contraction that allows the heart to work as a unit) begins with the pacemaker cells. This group of cells is self-excitable and able to depolarize to threshold and fire action potentials on their own, a feature called autorhythmicity; they do this at set intervals which determine heart rate. Because they are connected with gap junctions to surrounding muscle fibres and the specialized fibres of the heart’s conduction system, the pacemaker cells are able to transfer the depolarization to the other cardiac muscle fibres in a manner that allows the heart to contract in a coordinated manner.

Please note that unlike in skeletal muscle, one action potential results in one heart beat. This is because the action potentials in cardiac cells are prolonged, preventing a quick twitch from occurring. This is an important mechanism for producing myocyte contraction, as tetanus in myocytes would be dangerous (if held too long).

slides.title: Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 3: Cardiac muscle tissue

Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release:
extracellular Ca2+ enters through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
Ca2+-gated (ligand-gated) channels allow release of Ca2+ from SR
relaxation involves Ca2+ being pumped back into SR and out of cell

Calcium-mediated calcium release in cardiac myocytes. Credit: David Nascari and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Calcium-induced calcium release

In cardiac cells, unlike skeletal muscles, extracellular calcium is required to initiate release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The sarcoplasmic reticulum in cardiac muscle fibres is simpler than that of skeletal muscle fibres, and there is no direct physical link between proteins in the T-tubule and proteins in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane, so depolarization of the T-tubule membrane cannot directly cause calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Instead, cardiac muscle cells have voltage-gated calcium channels in the sarcolemma and along the T-tubules that open when the membrane is depolarized, allowing calcium to enter the cardiac muscle fibre from the extracellular fluid. This calcium then causes the opening of calcium-gated calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane that release additional calcium into the sarcoplasm.

slides.title: Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: And finally, we move on to Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue.

slides.title: Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue

Smooth muscle histology:
no striations because no sarcomeres
but do have thick and thin filaments composed of myosin and actin
spindle-shaped
shorter than skeletal muscle
uninucleate
found as interconnected cells in sheets in walls of hollow organs (bladder, uterus, GI tract, respiratory passageways, etc.)
found as single cells in muscles of eye, and skin (goosebumps - arrector pili muscle)

Smooth Muscle Tissue. Smooth muscle tissue is found around organs in the digestive, respiratory, reproductive tracts and the iris of the eye. LM × 1600. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Smooth muscle, so named because the cells do not have striations, is present in the walls of hollow organs like the urinary bladder, uterus, stomach, intestines, and in the walls of passageways, such as the arteries and veins of the circulatory system, and the tracts of the respiratory, urinary, and reproductive systems. Smooth muscle is also present in the eyes, where it functions to change the size of the iris and alter the shape of the lens. It is also present in the skin where it causes hair to stand erect in response to cold temperature or fear.

Smooth muscle fibres are spindle-shaped (wide in the middle and tapered at both ends, somewhat like a football) and have a single nucleus; they range from about 30 to 200 μm (thousands of times shorter than skeletal muscle fibres).

slides.title: Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue

Smooth muscle histology, continued:
thin filaments tethered to dense bodies (analogous to Z-discs)
during contraction, myosin pulls on actin
actin anchored to dense bodies (instead of Z-disc, as in sarcomeres)
dense bodies connected to network of intermediate filaments, so causes large contraction of whole fibre

Actin and myosin within smooth muscle fibres. Credit: Boumphreyfr, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Smooth Muscle Contraction. The dense bodies and intermediate filaments are networked through the sarcoplasm, which cause the muscle fibre to contract.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Although they do not have striations and sarcomeres, smooth muscle fibres do have thick and thin filaments composed of myosin and actin contractile proteins. These thin filaments are anchored by dense bodies. A dense body is analogous to the Z-discs of skeletal and cardiac muscle fibres and is tethered, or fastened, to the sarcolemma. 

The thin filaments are anchored to the dense bodies, which also have cord-like intermediate filaments attached to them. In fact, intermediate filaments appear as a network throughout the sarcoplasm and are connected to each other through dense bodies. Thus, as the thin filaments slide past the thick filaments, they pull on the dense bodies, which in turn pull on the network of intermediate filaments throughout the sarcoplasm. This arrangement causes the entire muscle fibre to contract in a manner which sees its ends being pulled toward the center.

slides.title: Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue

Calcium source:
Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release like in (cardiac muscle)
no troponin, so contraction not regulated by troponin-tropomyosin
instead, regulatory protein calmodulin binds calcium
calcium-calmodulin complex then activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) enzyme
phosphorylates myosin heads
hydrolyzes ATP, adds Pi to head
activated heads pull actin
calcium pumps restore Ca2+
leads to muscle relaxation
some Ca2+ remains to provide tone
e.g., in blood vessels
can thus contract OR dilate

Calcium-mediated calcium release in smooth muscle. Credit: David Nascari and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Calcium ions are supplied by calcium-induced calcium release, as in cardiac myocytes.

Because smooth muscle cells do not contain troponin, cross-bridge formation is not regulated by the troponin-tropomyosin complex but instead by the regulatory protein calmodulin. In a smooth muscle fibre, external calcium ions passing through opened calcium channels in the sarcolemma, and additional calcium released from SR, bind to calmodulin. The calcium-calmodulin complex then activates an enzyme called myosin light chain kinase, which, in turn, activates the myosin heads by phosphorylating them (converting ATP to ADP and Pi, with the Pi attaching to the head). The myosin heads can then attach to actin-binding sites and pull on the thin actin filaments. 

Muscle contraction continues until ATP-dependent calcium pumps actively transport calcium ions back into the SR and out of the cell. However, a low concentration of calcium remains in the sarcoplasm to maintain muscle tone. This remaining calcium keeps the muscle slightly contracted, which is important in certain tracts and around blood vessels, which can then either contract or dilate from this baseline, allowing for increased ability to regulate blood flow.

slides.title: Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue

Latched state:
slow and (individually) weak contractions – preserves ATP
tone, and contraction also maintained by latch-bridges, where myosin and actin stay coupled without Ca2+ presence until a phosphatase enzyme removes the phosphate group from myosin heads
e.g., in sphincters that stay tightened most of time

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Sphincters utilize latched-state smooth muscle. Credit: Jonathan Dyhr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
slides.notes: Because most smooth muscles must function for long periods without rest, their power output is relatively low and they contract slowly, but contractions can continue without using large amounts of energy. Some smooth muscle can also maintain contractions even as calcium is removed and myosin kinase is inactivated (or dephosphorylated). This can happen because a subset of cross-bridges between myosin heads and actin, called latch-bridges, keep the thick and thin filaments linked together for a prolonged period, and without the need for ATP. This allows for the maintaining of muscle “tone” in smooth muscle that lines arterioles and other visceral organs with very little energy expenditure. An example is the pyloric sphincter, shown in this image, which stays closed most of the time, except when allowing small amounts of chyme (food and digestive juices) from the stomach to the small intestine.

slides.title: Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue

Involuntary control:
local factors (e.g., localized histamine release, pH levels, stretch) 
hormones
neural stimulation (autonomic nervous system) – from varicosities (swellings along axons that result in less specific localization of released neurotransmitter than at neuromuscular junction)
acetylcholine
e.g., contraction of respiratory airways
norepinephrine
e.g., relaxation of respiratory airways
e.g., contraction of blood vessels
(opposite effects depend on tissue and/or the variant of receptor on cells)

Motor Units. A series of axon-like swelling, called varicosities or “boutons,” from autonomic neurons form motor units through the smooth muscle.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Smooth muscle is not under voluntary control; thus, it is called involuntary muscle. The triggers for smooth muscle contraction include hormones, neural stimulation by the autonomic nervous system releasing neurotransmitters from axonal varicosities, and local factors (e.g., localized histamine release, pH levels, and stretch – such as when food is present within the GI tract and distends it).

Different autonomic nerves release various neurotransmitters onto smooth muscle. For example, some nerves release acetylcholine that causes contraction of smooth muscle around some respiratory ducts and thus constriction of these airways. Other nerves release norepinephrine that causes relaxation of smooth muscle and thus widening of the airways. The same neurotransmitter can even cause opposite effects depending partly on the tissue where it acts and/or the variant of neurotransmitter receptor on target cells. Although norepinephrine causes relaxation of smooth muscle and thus widening of some airways, it also causes contraction of smooth muscle and thus constriction of most blood vessels.  Autonomic neurons innervating smooth muscle release their neurotransmitters from swellings along their axons, called varicosities, that tend to result in less specific localization of the released neurotransmitter than at a neuromuscular junction.

slides.title: Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 4: Smooth muscle tissue

Peristalsis. Credit: Auawise, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Peristalsis
slow, steady contractions
e.g., propels food through digestive tract
e.g., urine through ureters
Single-unit
cells joined by gap junctions
coordinates contraction
e.g., smooth muscle sheets
Multi-unit
cells regulated individually
e.g., muscles of the eye

Single-unit smooth muscle. Credit: Boumphreyfr, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Smooth muscle arranged in layers around a hollow organ generally produces slow, steady contractions known as peristalsis that allow substances, such as food in the digestive tract, to move through the body. Movement of substances through lumens by peristalsis occurs in some organs (the uterus, urinary bladder, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestines) and ducts (ureters, uterine tubes, vas deferens, bile ducts, etc.).

The coordinated manner of contraction that leads to peristalsis, and other forms of coordinated smooth muscle contraction, is due to gap junctions being present between cells of such types of smooth muscle, allowing depolarization to spread from one cell to another. These types of smooth muscles are called single-unit smooth muscle, because all of the cells function as part of a single unit. Smooth muscles that are controlled individually, such as those in the eye, are referred to as multi-unit smooth muscle.
